Seasonal fashion collection

Good local decisions can still create a poor overall result

A fashion retailer has launched a seasonal clothing collection. Some stores are selling out quickly, while others have too much stock. The challenge is not simply to work harder—it is to connect information and decisions across the whole supply chain.

The business situation

Sales sees strong demand in several locations. The warehouse still follows the original allocation plan. Finance wants to avoid expensive emergency transport. The supplier continues producing the original quantities. Each action seems reasonable alone, but the combined result is stockouts in some stores and excess inventory in others.

  • 1
    Demand signals

    Store-level sales and inventory data show where customer demand is actually changing.

  • 2
    Coordinated response

    Sales, Product Management, the Warehouse, Supplier, and Logistics must adjust together.

  • 3
    Overall performance

    Better orchestration improves availability, reduces excess stock, and speeds up the response.

Your task: Work through four short decisions and turn separate local actions into one coordinated end-to-end response.

Turn separate actions into one response

Local decisions Decision 1 of 4

Key takeaway

Orchestration improves the whole system

Supply-chain performance improves when customer signals, inventory decisions, supplier actions, and transport priorities are connected around one shared outcome.

Share real demand

Store-level demand and stock data should replace assumptions based only on the original forecast.

Coordinate inventory and supply

Reallocate existing stock first, then adjust supplier production using the new demand information.

Prioritize where it matters

Transport should respond to urgency rather than treating every location exactly the same.

Practical lesson: A department can make a sensible local choice that harms the total system. Orchestration means linking information, decisions, and actions so that the whole supply chain—not one function—performs better.
